Seven operating stages

Read every stage below. Select “Show this animation” to see its energy flow above.

STAGE 1 OF 7

Power the home and charge the battery

The panels generate 5 kW of DC power. The hybrid inverter supplies 2 kW of AC power to appliances, while its DC/DC battery stage sends the remaining 3 kW into storage.

5 kW solar = 2 kW appliances + 3 kW battery charging.

Inside the inverter

Two jobs happen together: DC → AC for the home, and controlled DC → DC for battery charging.

STAGE 2 OF 7

Send unused solar energy to the grid

The battery is full. Solar power supplies the home, and the remaining 3 kW passes through the bidirectional meter to the grid, where export is permitted.

5 kW solar = 2 kW appliances + 3 kW grid export.

Inside the inverter

DC → AC. The inverter synchronises with the grid so surplus AC power can flow out.

STAGE 3 OF 7

Run appliances from the battery

After sunset the solar panels produce no power. The battery releases stored energy as DC; the inverter converts it into AC to supply the home.

2 kW battery discharge = 2 kW appliances.

Inside the inverter

Battery DC → regulated DC link → switched and filtered AC for household appliances.

STAGE 4 OF 7

Combine solar, battery and grid power

Appliance demand is 5 kW. Solar contributes 1 kW and the battery supplies 2 kW through the inverter. The grid supplies the remaining 2 kW directly to the AC bus.

1 kW solar + 2 kW battery + 2 kW grid = 5 kW appliances.

Inside the inverter

Solar and battery DC are converted to AC. Grid AC joins the supply at the distribution board.

STAGE 5 OF 7

Charge the battery from the grid

Where supported and enabled, the grid supplies 3 kW: 1 kW runs appliances directly and 2 kW enters the hybrid inverter to charge the battery.

3 kW grid import = 1 kW appliances + 2 kW battery charging.

Inside the inverter

The bidirectional power stage operates as an AC → DC converter, with controlled battery charging.

STAGE 6 OF 7

Supply a separated backup installation

The grid connection is open. A backup-capable inverter establishes the local AC supply for selected circuits, using 1 kW of solar power and 1 kW from the battery. No power flows into the public network.

1 kW solar + 1 kW battery = 2 kW selected backup loads. Open grid connection = island mode.

Inside the inverter

The inverter establishes local voltage and frequency. Suitable transfer switching, system referencing and protection are essential.

STAGE 7 OF 7

A battery does not automatically provide backup

This comparison represents a system without enabled island capability. Its grid-parallel generation disconnects after loss of mains. The appliances shown lose supply, even though energy remains in the battery.

Stored energy + ordinary grid-connected operation ≠ an automatic backup supply.

Inside the inverter

No AC supply is established for these loads. Anti-islanding prevents unintended energisation of the public network.

Inside the inverter

Electronic switches rapidly reverse the DC voltage using pulse-width modulation. An output filter smooths the switching waveform into a near-sinusoidal AC output. When grid-connected, control synchronises the output with the grid.

KEY CONCEPT

What is a bidirectional device?

Bidirectional means that power can flow in either direction through a device. In this hybrid inverter, the bidirectional power-conversion stage can transfer energy between the DC side (battery) and the AC side (home and grid).

1 · DC → AC: discharging

Battery → inverter → appliances

The battery supplies DC electricity. The inverter converts it into AC electricity to run household appliances. A suitable system may also export battery energy to the grid where enabled and permitted.

2 · AC → DC: charging

Grid → converter → battery

When grid charging is supported and enabled, the same bidirectional stage works as a controlled rectifier: it converts AC into DC. Battery charging is regulated to suit the battery’s limits and state of charge.

Remember: “inverter” describes DC-to-AC conversion; “rectifier” describes AC-to-DC conversion. A bidirectional inverter/converter performs both functions, using electronic switches and control circuits.

The battery’s DC/DC interface can also be bidirectional: it controls power into the battery when charging and out of the battery when discharging. Solar-to-battery charging remains DC → DC in this system.

Two directions does not mean both at once. The illustrated conversion stage has one net power direction at a given moment. The home can still receive grid power while the battery charges because the home is connected to the AC distribution bus.

Connect the animation to the 18th Edition

BS 7671:2018+A4:2026 is the current 18th Edition text. The IET confirms the previous transition period ended on 15 October 2026. Amendment 4 includes a new battery chapter and consolidates Amendment 3. Use the current text when checking requirements.

IET: current edition and transition · IET/BSI: published Amendment 4

1 · Operating modes: connected is different from islanded

A prosumer both produces and consumes electricity. A PEI is a prosumer electrical installation. An EEMS is an electrical energy management system; it coordinates how available energy is used.

TermMeaning in the teaching exampleScene
Connected modeThe grid connection remains available; import or export may occur.1–5
Direct feedingPower is taken from the public network to help supply the installation.4–5
Reverse feedingSurplus local generation supplies power to the public network.2
No exchange / self-consumptionLocal sources meet demand, but the grid connection remains closed.1 and 3
Island modeThe supplied local circuits are separated from the grid and supplied by local sources.6
Classroom question: Scene 3 shows zero grid exchange. Is it islanded? No. The grid switch remains closed. In Scene 6 the switch is open and a local supply is established.

These are simplified teaching descriptions of power exchange. The open contact in the main diagram represents the grid connection function; it is not a drawing of the required conductor arrangement.

2 · Intentional islanding versus anti-islanding

Anti-islanding prevents local generation from continuing to energise the public network after mains failure. Intentional islanding supplies a deliberately separated local installation with suitable backup equipment.

Example: a fridge and lighting may be backed up while a cooker remains outside the backup circuits. A 3 kW backup output cannot supply a 7 kW cooking load; battery energy also limits operating time. At an idealised constant 1 kW load, 5 kWh of usable energy lasts about 5 hours, before losses and reserve allowances.

Compare Scenes 6 and 7: one establishes a separate supply; the other loses appliance power. Neither exports into a failed grid. Backup capability, automatic transfer and uninterrupted supply are separate product features.

3 · Earthing and transfer switching

For the illustrated residential arrangement, island operation commonly establishes TN-S. A local earth electrode is needed; the distributor’s earthing provision cannot be the sole basis of the island arrangement.

All live grid conductors serving the island, including neutral, are separated. A controlled neutral-to-protective-conductor reference provides the metallic earth-fault return path. The electrode provides the Earth reference; it does not replace the CPC.

  1. Leave connected mode: disconnect the relevant grid live conductors.
  2. Establish the island system reference with interlocked switching.
  3. Supply the selected circuits from the local source.
  4. Return: remove the island reference before reconnecting the grid, following the equipment’s controlled sequence.

The grid protective-earth connection is not shown as a switched conductor. This conceptual sequence is not a wiring instruction for adding a permanent neutral–earth link.

IET: earthing principles and transfer sequence (older guidance; read with A4 and the current article below).

4 · Current terminology and fault protection

PCE: power conversion equipment. SRC: system referencing conductor. SRCSD: the switch controlling that reference. SDFI: switching device for islanding; it separates the local installation from the network. SDFI and SRCSD functions are interlocked; Regulation 826.1.1.5 addresses suitability for isolation.

Inverter fault current is limited, so normal MCB operation cannot simply be assumed. Island ADS needs appropriate RCD protection, downstream of the system reference. Selection must suit both converter and loads. Regulation 570.6.2.2 addresses converter-related RCD type; 531.3.3 addresses load compatibility.

Check ADS in both modes. A conventional loop reading alone does not establish inverter fault behaviour; 826.7 allows alternative verification. Use manufacturer evidence and suitable inspection/testing.

IET July 2026: island-mode ADS and current terminology.

5 · Bidirectional inverter ≠ bidirectional protective device

The inverter converts energy in either direction. A bidirectional protective device is designed to remain suitable when either side can be supplied. It does not perform AC/DC conversion.

During grid charging, the grid is the source. During battery discharge or solar export, the inverter is another source. Some electronic RCBOs or AFDDs can be damaged by unsuitable reverse supply conditions. Check the manufacturer’s declared suitability, terminal markings and installation instructions; appearance alone does not prove suitability.

RCD Type B describes residual-current waveform sensitivity. Type B MCB describes an overcurrent trip characteristic. Neither phrase by itself means “bidirectional”.

IET: protective-device directionality · IET: original Amendment 3 provision (now consolidated into A4).

Design link: energy-flow animation explains operation. Compliance also depends on equipment ratings, protection, earthing, transfer arrangements and verification in every permitted mode. The references above are study signposts; the full current standard and equipment instructions determine the design.

What the animation represents

A simplified DC-coupled hybrid system. Solar and battery connections are DC; appliances and the grid use AC. Solar-to-battery charging uses controlled DC/DC conversion; it does not need to become AC first.

Numbers are illustrative power values; conversion losses are omitted so the power balance is easy to follow. Battery percentages illustrate each scene rather than a timed battery model. Actual priorities depend on settings, battery limits and export permissions.

During a grid failure: normal grid-connected operation disconnects from the grid. Backup requires suitable equipment and a safely separated backup circuit; a battery alone does not guarantee backup power.

Further reading: US Department of Energy — power electronics · Australian Government — inverters · Inverters and grid services

AC → DC · FOLLOW THE WAVEFORM

Rectifiers: how AC becomes DC in everyday equipment

An inverter converts DC into AC. A rectifier converts AC into DC. Understanding both explains how a hybrid inverter can discharge a battery to supply appliances and reverse the energy transfer to charge it from the grid.

Input: alternating voltage

AC reverses polarity every half-cycle. In the UK, a 50 Hz supply completes 50 cycles per second. This animation is slowed down for teaching.

Output: half-wave pulsating DC

DC does not have to be perfectly flat. Rectified voltage can pulse while retaining the same polarity. The rise and fall remaining on a DC output is called ripple. These normalised waveforms illustrate shape, not a mains-voltage design; diode drops, source impedance and switching details are omitted.

What happens inside each rectifier?

StageHow it worksAt 50 Hz input
Half-wave · one diodeA diode conducts when forward-biased and blocks the opposite half-cycle. The illustrated load receives positive pulses with gaps between them.50 output pulses per second.
Full-wave bridge · four diodesOne pair conducts during one half-cycle; the other pair conducts during the next. The bridge routes both halves so conventional current through a resistive load has the same direction. Two diodes are in the conducting path.100 output pulses per second; ripple frequency is 100 Hz.
Capacitor across the outputThe capacitor charges near the peaks and supplies the load between peaks. Its voltage falls as it discharges, leaving ripple. Increasing capacitance or reducing load current generally reduces ripple.For the smoothed full-wave example, the recharge pattern repeats at 100 Hz.

Waveform and diode principles: Analog Devices: half-wave and bridge rectification · Analog Devices: power supplies and smoothing · MPS: uncontrolled rectifiers.

How this connects to the hybrid inverter

A basic diode bridge is a one-way AC-to-DC converter. It cannot, by itself, send battery power back as AC. A bidirectional hybrid inverter typically uses actively controlled semiconductor switches: the power stage can operate as an inverter in one direction and as a controlled rectifier in the other. Product topologies vary.

Operating taskEnergy pathConversion
Charge from grid ACGrid → controlled rectifier / DC link → regulated battery interface → batteryAC → DC, followed by battery charging control.
Discharge battery to appliancesBattery → DC link → inverter → AC distributionDC → AC.
Charge battery from solar in this DC-coupled systemSolar panels → controlled DC/DC stage → batteryDC → DC; grid rectification is not required.

Rectification alone is not battery charging control. A charger must regulate suitable voltage and current, coordinate with the battery management system (BMS), and respond to operating limits. A smoothing capacitor alone does not make a safe battery charger.

Charging stages: onsemi: AC-input battery-charger stages. Bidirectional conversion: US Department of Energy: power electronic devices.

Link to the 18th Edition: converter operation helps explain why protective-device directionality and residual-current waveform compatibility are separate checks. Revisit the Chapter 57, Chapter 82 and protective-device discussion below. A rectifier does not provide grid isolation; that is the role of the appropriate switching arrangements.

Rectifiers in everyday appliances

Many appliances receive AC at the plug but use DC internally. Rectification is one stage in a power supply; voltage conversion, filtering and regulation perform other jobs.

ExampleTypical energy conversionWhy rectification is needed
Phone or tablet wall adapterMains AC → rectified DC → high-frequency isolated conversion → regulated USB DC.Produces a suitable DC supply for the device. The phone’s charging electronics then manage its battery.
Television, router or laptop adapterMains AC → internal switched-mode supply → regulated DC rails.Processors and other electronic circuits need controlled DC voltages. Different circuits may need different rails.
LED lightingMains AC → AC/DC driver → controlled LED current.LEDs conduct primarily in one direction and need current control; a bridge alone does not regulate LED current.
Inverter washing machineMains AC → rectifier → DC-link capacitor → motor inverter → motor.The DC link supplies an inverter that controls motor speed and torque. The motor is not simply connected to the rectifier output.
Variable-speed refrigerator or air conditionerAC input → DC link → inverter-controlled compressor motor.Allows variable-speed operation. This describes inverter-driven models; conventional motor arrangements differ.

Manufacturer examples: TI: television power supplies · TI: AC-input LED driver · Infineon: washing-machine power conversion · Infineon: appliance motor inverter.

Follow the power through a mobile-phone charger

A typical isolated switched-mode wall adapter uses more than a bridge rectifier. Select each stage:

1 · Mains AC enters the adapter

The wall socket supplies AC. The adapter contains input protection and interference filtering before its conversion stages.

Important distinction: the wall adapter supplies regulated DC; the phone manages how that supply charges its battery. USB-C Power Delivery can negotiate a supported voltage and power level rather than always using one fixed output.

The block sequence is representative. Modern designs may use active or bridgeless input stages and different isolation topologies.

onsemi: USB-C AC-input power-supply stages.

Why convert AC → DC → high-frequency AC → DC? The first rectifier creates a DC bus. Fast switching lets a compact transformer transfer energy and provide isolation. The secondary stage then creates the controlled DC output. These stages have different purposes.

Two useful classroom comparisons

Washing machine: rectifier first, inverter second. The rectifier makes a DC link; the inverter uses that link to drive the motor with controlled AC.

Solar battery system: inverter operation supplies AC appliances from battery DC. During grid charging, controlled rectifier operation transfers AC energy into the DC system. Neither conversion changes whether the SDFI is open or closed by itself.

Remember: not every load needs rectification. A simple resistive heating element can run directly from AC; any electronic controls may have a separate DC power supply.

These are functional teaching sequences, not service or construction instructions. Mains-side DC-link capacitors may retain hazardous voltage after disconnection.
